english: to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')
usage: to be quick on the uptake
The whole idiom; 눈치 takes 가, never 를, with 빠르다. To pay a compliment to a friend: 너 진짜 눈치 빠르다 — to a senior: 눈치가 빠르시네요.
to catch on / pick up on something
Here 눈치 takes 를 — sensing a hidden fact, e.g. 선물인 걸 눈치챘어 ('I caught on it was a gift'). This is the moment of realizing, not the standing trait.
Watching a person's face to gauge their reaction; can sound timid or subservient, e.g. 상사 눈치를 보다 ('keep checking the boss's mood') — not a compliment.
The direct opposite — missing social cues entirely; 눈치 없이 끼어들다 = butt in without reading the room. 눈치(가) 보이다 is yet another: 'to feel self-conscious / sense I'm being judged.'
examples: 우리 강아지는 눈치가 빨라.
Our dog is quick to read the mood.
Simplest frame: subject + 눈치가 빨라; works even for pets, who sense your mood — shows the idiom isn't limited to clever people.
A: 나 아무 말도 안 했는데 어떻게 알았어? / B: 딱 보면 알지, 내가 눈치가 좀 빨라.
A: I didn't say a word — how'd you know? / B: I can just tell; I'm pretty perceptive.
A/B turn: 딱 보면 알지 ('I can tell at a glance') is the natural brag that pairs with 눈치가 빠르다 when someone reads you without being told.
여기선 눈치가 빨라야 살아남아요.
Around here you've got to be quick on the uptake to survive.
Real office-survival nuance; 눈치가 빨라야 = 'you must be perceptive' (the -아야 'must' frame), hinting that Korean workplaces reward reading unspoken cues.
nuance: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. You say it about a friend, a sharp junior at work, even a perceptive child, and it is safe across registers: 너 눈치 빠르다 to a friend, 눈치가 빠르시네요 to someone you respect. Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — a person can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). Its nearest sibling expression 분위기 파악을 잘하다 ('reads the atmosphere well') overlaps but is more about group situations, whereas 눈치 빠르다 also covers reading one individual. Forms range from the bare brag 눈치 빠르다 up to honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요, and it pairs habitually with 금방 알아채다 (notice right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다.

structuredNuance.t: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. It pairs habitually with 분위기를 파악하다 (grasp the atmosphere) and 금방 알아채다 (notice right away).

Use it as praise — about a friend, a sharp junior, a perceptive child. It works at every level: casual 너 눈치 빠르다 to a friend, honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요 to someone senior. There is no register danger here; it is almost always welcome because it flatters someone's social intelligence. The only caution is tone — said sarcastically (눈치 빠르네…) about someone who exploited a cue, it can turn into a jab.

Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — one can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). Its sibling expression 분위기 파악을 잘하다 leans toward reading a group's mood, while 눈치 빠르다 also covers reading one person; 센스 있다 ('to have sense') is the warmer, more general cousin for thoughtful tact.

Scale from the bare brag 눈치 빠르다, to polite 눈치가 빨라요, to honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요. Switch the particle to shift meaning entirely: 눈치를 채다 (catch on to a fact), 눈치를 보다 (anxiously gauge someone), 눈치가 없다 (oblivious — the opposite), 눈치가 보이다 (feel self-conscious about onlookers).

The big pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다. English has no single word for 눈치, so don't force 'tactful' or 'clever' onto it — it is its own concept of cue-reading.

mistakes: Don't translate it as 'fast eyes' or link it to good vision — 눈치 means reading social atmosphere, despite containing 눈 ('eye'). It is mental/social, never about how well you physically see.
Particle error: people say 눈치를 빠르다, but the idiom is 눈치'가' 빠르다 because 빠르다 is an adjective. Use 를 only with the action verbs 채다/보다 (눈치를 채다 = catch on).

눈치가 빠르다 (perceptive, a compliment) ≠ 눈치를 보다 (nervously watching someone's reaction, often timid/subservient). They are not interchangeable and carry opposite vibes — one praises sharpness, the other hints at anxiety.

english: to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')
usage: The full idiom; 발 takes 이/은, and the adjective is 넓다 ('wide'). 발이 참 넓으시네요 = polite admiration of someone's reach.
a well-connected person / a social hub
Attributive 넓은 + noun; the go-to way to describe a networker who knows everybody and can connect people.
The opposite ('narrow feet') — knowing hardly anyone; 나는 발이 좁아서 = 'I don't know many people, so…' (a humble self-deprecation).
Near-synonym EXPRESSION using 인맥 (人脈, 'people-vein'); slightly more formal/business-flavored than the warmer, idiomatic 발이 넓다.
examples: 우리 삼촌은 발이 넓어요.
My uncle knows a lot of people.
Plain frame: subject + 발이 넓어요; states the trait neutrally as a simple fact about someone.
일자리 알아보는 거면 발 넓은 선배한테 물어봐.
If you're job-hunting, ask that senior who knows everyone.
Everyday: drop 이 in casual speech (발 넓은) and tap a connector for help — the idiom's most practical use is pointing to a useful person.
A: 그 사람 소개 좀 받을 수 있을까? / B: 민수한테 부탁해 봐, 걔가 발이 넓잖아.
A: Could you get me an introduction to them? / B: Try asking Minsu — you know he's super well-connected.
A/B turn: 걔가 발이 넓잖아 ('he's well-connected, you know') is exactly how Koreans steer you to the person who can introduce you.
nuance: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach, used when someone seems to know people everywhere or could get you an introduction; register is neutral, fine in casual 발 넓네 and polite 발이 넓으시네요 alike, and there is no one you'd offend by saying it. Its sharper near-synonym expression is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein,' a Sino-Korean word picturing connections as veins) names the network explicitly and sounds a touch more formal or business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer, more idiomatic everyday version, while 마당발 ('wide-foot person') is the noun nickname for such a connector. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions). The key English-speaker pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy Koreans would say 친한 친구가 많다 instead. The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions), 마당발이다 (be a connector).

Use it admiringly when someone seems to know people everywhere or could connect you to others. Register is neutral and safe: 발 넓네 to a friend, 발이 넓으시네요 to someone senior. It is a flattering observation, so there's no one it would offend — though if said with a wry tone it can imply 'always out networking,' so let context stay friendly.

Its sharper near-synonym expression is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein') names the network explicitly and sounds more formal/business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer everyday version. The noun nickname for such a person is 마당발 ('wide-foot'), as in 걔는 완전 마당발이야. None of these imply close friendship — only reach.

Shift the adjective for the antonym: 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet' = few connections). Use the attributive 발 넓은 사람 to describe someone, the noun 마당발 to nickname them, and 인맥이 넓다 for a more formal phrasing. Honorific: 발이 넓으시다.

The key pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy say 친한 친구가 많다. The opposite is 발이 좁다, not 발이 작다 ('small feet').

mistakes: It has nothing to do with literal foot size; never read 발이 넓다 as a physical description of someone's feet.
Don't use it for close friendships — it means a wide circle of ACQUAINTANCES, not many best friends. For that, say 친한 친구가 많다. Breadth, not depth.
The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다 ('small feet'). Picking the antonym by literal size breaks the idiom.

english: to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')
usage: Full idiom; 손 takes 이, adjective is 크다 ('big'). 우리 엄마 손 커 = my mom always makes/gives a lot of food.
Attributive 큰 + 사람; common compliment for a host who over-caters or a friend who always treats.
to be stingy / always prepare too little
Opposite ('small hands') — skimping on portions or money; 손이 작아서 늘 모자라 = always runs short at the table.
Verb collocation: 크게 쓰다 = lay out money freely on others, e.g. 오늘은 손 크게 쓸게 ('I'll splurge today / it's on me').
examples: 우리 엄마는 손이 커요.
My mom is generous (cooks a lot).
Plain frame; defaults to the cooking-amount reading — she always makes far more than needed.
손이 크신 분이라 선물도 늘 푸짐해요.
She's generous, so her gifts are always lavish.
Everyday: honorific 크신 + 푸짐하다 (plentiful) — shows the idiom extends from food to gift-giving generosity.
A: 이걸 다 어떻게 먹어, 다섯 명인데! / B: 엄마가 손이 크셔서 항상 이래.
A: How are we supposed to eat all this — there's only five of us! / B: Mom's so generous with food, it's always like this.
A/B turn: the classic Korean dinner-table moment; 손이 크셔서 항상 이래 explains the overflowing table with fond exasperation.
nuance: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance (a 손 큰 host would rather over-cater than run short), and you say it fondly about a mother, a relative, or a friend who always treats; register is neutral-to-positive, safe in 손 크다 with friends and 손이 크시다 with elders. Contrast it with 인심이 좋다 ('good 인심/人心, human-heartedness'), a near-synonym expression that stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy; 통이 크다 ('big container') is yet another sibling but means bold/big-spirited about money and decisions, not food portions. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful), 회식 때 많이 사 주다 (treats a lot at company dinners). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others; and don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker), which is unrelated. Opposite: 손이 작다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful).

Said fondly about someone who feeds or gives generously — a mom who over-caters, a friend who always treats. Register is neutral-to-positive: casual 손 크다, honorific 손이 크시다 for an elder. It is praise, so it lands warmly in any company, and it's a graceful way to thank a generous host without sounding stiff.

Contrast it with the near-synonym expression 인심이 좋다 ('good human-heartedness'), which stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy. 통이 크다 ('big container') is a third sibling — bold/big-spirited about money and decisions, not food portions.
Flip to 손이 작다 ('small hands') for the stingy/under-preparing opposite. Use 손이 큰 사람 to describe a host, and the verb phrase 손 크게 쓰다 ('spend big') when picking up a generous tab. Honorific: 손이 크시다.

It is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others. And don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker) or 손버릇이 나쁘다 ('bad hand-habit' = thieving), both unrelated body-part idioms.

mistakes: Not about literal hand size, and not about splurging on yourself — it's specifically generosity toward others (cooking/giving in big amounts). 'Big-handed' in English carries no such meaning.
Don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = quick, efficient at a task). Different idiom, different meaning — speed, not generosity.
The opposite is 손이 작다 ('small hands' = stingy/under-prepares), not 손이 짧다 (which evokes 'short arms,' a separate image about being slow to give/help).

english: to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')
usage: Full idiom; 입 takes 이, adjective 무겁다 ('heavy'). 그 사람 입 무거워 = you can trust them with a secret.
a discreet person you can trust with secrets
Attributive 무거운 + 사람; the phrase that vouches for someone's reliability before you confide in them.
Opposite ('light mouth') — can't keep anything quiet; 걔 입 가벼워, 말하지 마 = don't tell, they'll leak it.
to shut one's mouth / keep quiet
Related verb; 다물다 = the concrete act of staying silent about a specific thing, e.g. 그 일은 입 다물고 있어 ('keep quiet about that').
examples: 우리 형은 입이 무거워.
My older brother is tight-lipped.
Plain frame; states a trustworthy trait — he won't repeat what you tell him.
이건 비밀인데, 너 입 무거운 거 알아서 말하는 거야.
This is a secret, but I'm telling you because I know you're discreet.
Everyday: drop 이 (입 무겁다) and use the phrase to vouch for the listener right before confiding.
A: 나 이거 말해도 돼? 소문나면 큰일인데. / B: 걱정 마, 나 입 진짜 무거워.
A: Can I tell you this? It'll be a disaster if it gets around. / B: Don't worry — I'm really good at keeping secrets.
A/B turn: 나 입 진짜 무거워 is the standard reassurance someone offers to be trusted with a secret.
nuance: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. It's a compliment, used to reassure someone before sharing something private (말해도 돼, 걔 입 무거워) or to vouch for a trustworthy colleague; register is neutral and works in both casual and polite settings, with no one it would offend. A crucial distinction: 입이 무겁다 is about confidentiality, NOT about being a quiet or shy personality in general — for that you'd say 말이 없다 ('has few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved, a literary-leaning word); a chatty, outgoing person can still be 입이 무거운 if they simply never leak. Its closest near-synonym expression is 입이 무거운 사람은 입단속을 잘한다 — the idiom 입단속을 잘하다 ('keep a tight lid on one's words'), which names the same discretion as an action, while the plain equivalent is simply 비밀을 잘 지키다. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Keep the body-part idioms straight: heavy/light mouth = discretion, not mouth size; and remember the particle is 이/은 (입이 무겁다), since 무겁다 is an adjective.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on).

Use it to reassure someone before they confide (걔 입 무거우니까 말해도 돼) or to vouch for a trustworthy colleague. Register is neutral — casual 입 무거워, polite 입이 무거우세요 — and it works in both work and personal settings without offending anyone. It is genuine praise of reliability.

It is about confidentiality, NOT general quietness — for shy/reserved use 말이 없다 ('few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved). A chatty, outgoing person can still be 입이 무거운 if they never leak confidences. The true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), not 입이 작다; 비밀을 잘 지키다 is the plain non-idiomatic equivalent.

Flip to 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = blabbermouth) for the opposite. Use 입이 무거운 사람 to describe someone, and the concrete verb 입을 다물다 ('shut one's mouth') for the act of staying silent about a specific thing. Honorific: 입이 무거우시다.

The pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Also note the particle: 무겁다 is an adjective, so it's 입'이' 무겁다, never the object marker 을.

mistakes: It's about keeping SECRETS, not about being quiet or shy by nature. A chatty person can still be 입이 무거운 if they never leak confidences; for 'quiet,' use 말이 없다 or 과묵하다.
The opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), not 입이 작다. Don't pick the antonym by literal mouth size.
Don't say 입을 무겁다 — 무겁다 is an adjective describing 입, so the particle is 이/은 (입이 무겁다), never the object marker 을. Use 을 only with the action verb 다물다.

english: to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')
usage: Full idiom; 귀 takes 가, adjective 얇다 ('thin'). 나 귀 얇아 = I cave to whatever I'm told.
Attributive 얇은 + 사람; mildly negative — they flip with the last opinion they heard.
to be on the gullible side
Softening 편이다 ('tend to be') makes the self-criticism gentler and less harsh — the polite way to admit it.
to be won over / fall for it
Frequent partner verb: 꼬시면 바로 넘어가 = caves the moment coaxed. It names the result of being 귀가 얇다.
examples: 나 귀가 얇아.
I'm easily swayed.
Simplest self-description with 귀가 얇다; often said half-jokingly to excuse an impulse purchase.
친구가 좋다고 하니까 귀가 얇아져서 같은 걸 샀어.
My friend said it was good, so I caved and bought the same thing.
Everyday: 귀가 얇아지다 (become swayed) in a shopping moment — the inchoative shows the swaying happening in real time.
A: 너 그거 또 샀어? 광고 보고 산 거지? / B: 어... 내가 귀가 좀 얇잖아.
A: You bought that too? You got it from an ad, didn't you? / B: Yeah… you know I'm a bit of a pushover.
A/B turn: 내가 귀가 좀 얇잖아 is the sheepish self-admission after an impulse buy.
nuance: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a harsh insult — Koreans cheerfully admit 나 귀 얇아, and you can safely tease a close friend with 너 귀 얇잖아, but be gentler with someone you don't know well since it does imply weak judgment. Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'): 순진하다 is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically the trait of being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may still hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. Its closest near-synonym expression is the playful noun 팔랑귀 ('fluttering ear'), which names exactly this trait — 너 완전 팔랑귀야 = 'you cave to anything.' Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over), 사기당하다 (get scammed). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about hearing ability or literally thin ears, and it must NOT be read as a compliment for being 'open-minded' or 'flexible' — it always implies a lack of one's own judgment; for genuine flexibility say 생각이 유연하다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over).

The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a cutting insult — Koreans freely say 나 귀 얇아 about themselves. You can tease a close friend (너 귀 얇잖아), but soften it (귀가 얇은 편이야) for someone you know less well, since it does imply weak judgment. Avoid saying it bluntly to a boss or stranger — it would sting.

Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'), which is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. 팔랑귀 ('fluttering ear') is the cuter noun nickname for exactly this trait.

Soften self-criticism with 귀가 얇은 편이다 ('tend to be on the gullible side'). Use the inchoative 귀가 얇아지다 ('got swayed') in the moment, the partner verb 넘어가다 ('be won over') for the result, and the playful noun 팔랑귀 to nickname someone.

english: to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')

Totally different idiom! 피우다, not 맞다 — don't confuse the two; 바람피웠어 = 'I cheated,' a dangerous slip.

Everyday: 기다리다가 sets the scene before the no-show; 결국 = 'in the end,' marking the let-down conclusion.

english: to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)

The grammar engine inside: verb + 는 줄 모르다, e.g. 비 오는 줄 몰랐어 ('didn't realize it was raining').
to not even notice time passing
Adding 도 ('even') intensifies the absorption — you were that lost in it that the clock vanished.
Natural partner adverb: 정신없이 놀다가 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어 = lost in fun, lost track of time.

Near-synonym with 흘리다 ('shed'); heard just as often, same flustered struggle, image of sweat pouring.

Intransitive variant: the sweat comes out on its own under pressure, no agent — 'I started sweating bullets.'
Cousin word; 식은땀 = literally 'cooled sweat,' from a scare or shock, not laborious struggle. 식은땀이 나다 = break into a fearful sweat.

english: to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic
usage: to catch one's breath / get a breather

Different idiom! Same 한숨 but 쉬다 = the act of sighing, often heavy with worry — not the relief of 돌리다.

Natural lead-in: handle the emergency first, then 한숨 돌리다 once the crisis eases. 급한 불 끄고 한숨 돌렸어.

Simple frame with 이제 ('now') marking the relief point right after the stress lifts.

english: for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')

It describes deflated excitement or mood, not a literal leak. Don't use 김이 새다 for actual gas, air, or water leaking (that's 새다 used plainly, e.g. 가스가 새다).
Don't over-narrow it to parties — for a shattered party mood specifically you can say 흥이 깨지다, but 김이 새다 covers any deflated anticipation, including quiet disappointment.

english: to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')
usage: to be eaten up with worry
Full idiom; 속 (insides) takes 이, verb 타다 ('burn'). 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타 = sick with worry over no reply.
to fret / to make someone worry
Causative 태우다 — either you fret, or you cause others worry; 부모 속을 태우다 = worry one's parents.
for worry to gnaw deeper and deeper
Intensified 타들어 가다 = the burning spreads inward; stronger and more drawn-out, the worst phase of dread.
Close synonym idiom with 애 (one's innards/heart): 애가 타 죽겠어 = I'm dying of anxiety.
examples: 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타.
I can't reach them and I'm worried sick.
Simple frame; 안 되다 (can't get through) triggers the worry — the unreachable-person scenario is the classic trigger.
합격 발표 기다리느라 속이 타요.
I'm on edge waiting for the results.
Everyday: -느라 names the anxious waiting as the cause; polite 요 form fits sharing real distress with someone.
A: 왜 이렇게 안절부절못해? / B: 애가 시험 보러 갔는데 연락이 없어서 속이 타 죽겠어.
A: Why are you so on edge? / B: My kid went to take an exam and hasn't called, so I'm worried sick.
A/B turn: 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of worry') is the hyperbolic peak you reach when waiting helplessly on someone.
nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry'): 걱정하다 is the everyday mental act of worrying, while 속이 타다 is the physical, churning agony of it, the way English 'worried SICK' outweighs 'worried.' Register is casual-to-polite and the feeling is genuine distress, so it's apt when you truly can't sit still, not for minor concerns. A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards/heart-strings), nearly identical in force, while 발을 동동 구르다 ('stamp one's feet') adds the restless, can't-stay-put body language. The key grammar is the 이/을 voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the burning anxiety (it happens to you), whereas the causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone else worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다 = a child makes the parents worry). Intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish (for a stomach ailment use 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다) — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying and who is causing the worry.

english: to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')
usage: to be jam-packed (no room to step)
Full idiom; mind the spacing: 발 디딜 (to step) + 틈이 없다 ('no gap'). 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어 = the shop is mobbed.
to have not even room to step
Swapping 이→도 ('even') heightens the crowding to extreme — not a sliver of space left.
The verb core; 디디다 = to plant your foot down, here modifying 틈 as the attributive 발 디딜.
Sino-Korean near-synonym EXPRESSION (人山人海, 'people-mountain-people-sea'); punchier and more dramatic, common in news.
examples: 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어.
The shop is jam-packed.
Simple frame; subject + 발 디딜 틈이 없어 — the plainest way to say a place is mobbed.
출근 시간 지하철은 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
The subway at rush hour has no room to even stand.
Everyday: 틈도 없다 intensifies the rush-hour crush; polite 요 form works in description or report.
A: 주말에 그 카페 갈까? / B: 거기 주말엔 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자.
A: Want to go to that cafe on the weekend? / B: It's totally packed there on weekends — let's go on a weekday.
A/B turn: 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자 is the real-life way to steer plans away from a crowded spot.
nuance: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with a crowd — usually with a slightly overwhelmed tone; register is casual-to-polite and works fine in conversation and writing alike. Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, literally 'people-mountain, people-sea'), a punchier four-character idiom for an enormous throng often seen in news and dramatic description; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational, everyday way to say it, while 미어터지다 ('to be bursting at the seams') is an even more colloquial sibling. The single most important thing to get right is spacing and the verb: it is 발 디딜 틈이 없다, where 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다, 'to set a foot down') modifies 틈 ('gap') — beginners wrongly fuse it as 발디딜. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, so don't use it for a room cluttered with objects — for that you'd better say 어질러져 있다 (it's a mess). Natural partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).

Used with a slightly overwhelmed tone to describe a crush of people. Register is casual-to-polite and fits both speech and writing — you can warn a friend (거기 발 디딜 틈도 없어) or describe a festival in a polite report. It is hyperbole, so reserve it for genuinely heavy crowds, not a moderately busy room.

Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, 'people-mountain, people-sea'), punchier and more dramatic, common in news; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational version. An even more colloquial sibling is 미어터지다 ('bursting at the seams'); 북적북적하다 is the milder 'bustling' for moderate crowds.
Word-for-word 'no gap to step' = utterly packed. Heighten it with 발 디딜 틈'도' 없다 ('not even room to step') or the adverbial 발 디딜 틈도 없이. Keep the spacing 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다) — never fuse to 발디딜.

Scope trap: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, not a room cluttered with objects — for clutter say 어질러져 있다 ('it's a mess'). And don't fuse the spelling: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다, with 발 디딜 (verb 디디다) kept separate, not 발디딜.

mistakes: Spacing/verb error: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (발 디딜 = 'to step,' from 발을 디디다), not the fused 발디딜. Keep the space and the verb 디디다.
It's specifically about crowds of PEOPLE, not a room cluttered with objects. For a messy, cluttered space use 어질러져 있다, not this crowd idiom.
Don't drop 틈: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 needs 틈 ('gap'). 발 디딜 데가 없다 exists but shifts nuance toward 'nowhere to step/stand,' so keep 틈이 없다 for the 'jam-packed' meaning.
